synthesis.title: Database indexing
synthesis.summary: How relational database indexes are structured, chosen and maintained.

sentences: B-tree indexes keep keys sorted, so they serve both equality and range lookups.
btree-order
Each B-tree node holds many keys, which keeps the tree shallow even for large tables.
btree-order
Hash indexes answer equality lookups in constant time but cannot serve ranges.
hash-lookup
A hash index gives no ordering, so it cannot help a sort.
hash-lookup
Bitmap indexes suit columns with few distinct values.
bitmap-low-cardinality
An index pays off on columns that filter out most rows.
selective-columns
A column with a handful of distinct values rarely benefits from a plain index.
selective-columns
In a composite index, the leftmost column decides which queries can use it.
composite-order
Equality columns belong before range columns in a composite index.
composite-order
A covering index answers a query without reading the table.
covering-index
Every index slows down inserts and updates because it must be kept in step with the table.
write-cost
Dropping unused indexes saves write time and disk space.
write-cost
Indexes grow sparse after many deletes and updates, which wastes pages.
index-bloat
Rebuilding a bloated index restores its compactness.
index-bloat
Table statistics must be refreshed so the planner picks the right index.
stats-refresh

members.claim: B-tree indexes keep their keys in sorted order in wide nodes.
Hash indexes map a key to a row location without keeping any order.
Bitmap indexes work well on columns with few distinct values.
Indexes help most on columns that filter out most rows.
A composite index is ordered by its columns from left to right.
An index that holds every column a query needs avoids reading the table.
Each index adds work to every write on its table.
Indexes accumulate unused space as rows are deleted and updated.
The planner relies on table statistics to choose among indexes.

dispute.fact: Benchmarks on current engines show B-tree indexes equal or faster for most equality workloads.
dispute.quote: B-tree lookups matched hash lookups in most of the measured workloads.

notes.claim: Indexes make every query faster.
notes.label: disputed

dispute.fact: Write-heavy queries run slower with more indexes.
dispute.quote: Each added index increased the time of every insert.
